questions.stem:
Read the two statements given below and answer the question that follows.
Statement: What we know today as Vedic literature existed in oral form for several centuries before it was written down.
Reason: The Vedas constitute the earliest known corpus of Indian literature especially because the script used by the Harappans of the Sindhu–Sarasvatī civilisation has been deciphered.
Which of the following options is correct? (A) Both the statement and the reason are true and the reason is a correct explanation of the statement. (B) Both the statement and the reason are true but the reason is not a correct explanation of the statement. (C) The statement is true but the reason is false. (D) Both the statement and the reason are false.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: The statement is true but the reason is false.

questions.stem: Set out, step by step, how rules and norms come into being when large groups of people live together, what a society is made up of, and how far Indian society had already organised itself in early times.

markingPoints.description: States that when large groups of people live together, rules and shared norms evolve over time to maintain order and harmony (1)
States that these rules and norms bind different social groups into a unified whole, forming a ‘system’ that helps organise and govern people effectively (1)
States that from early times Indian society developed several such systems of organisation based on existing customs, traditions, and agreed practices (1)
States that a society is a system of social relationships among individuals who share a common territory, culture, and a shared sense of belonging (1)
Names the structural units such as families or households, the institution such as marriage, and customs that provide a framework for individual and social life (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Step 1: Whenever large groups of people live together, certain rules and shared norms evolve over time to maintain order and harmony. Step 2: These rules and norms bind different social groups into a unified whole, forming a ‘system’ that helps organise and govern people effectively. Step 3: From early times, Indian society developed several such systems of organisation based on existing customs, traditions, and agreed practices. Step 4: A society is a system of social relationships among individuals who share a common territory, culture, and a shared sense of belonging. Step 5: It consists of structural units such as families or households, institutions such as marriage, and customs that provide a framework for individual and social life.

Step 5: Interestingly, both the Ṛigveda and the Sindhu–Sarasvatī civilisation were familiar with copper.

questions.stem:
A Class 9 teacher is worried about two words that students keep swapping. The first is used for people who share a common territory, a culture and a shared sense of belonging, and who settle their differences and pass on their ways of doing things. The second is used for an organised political system with rules and laws, clear rights and duties of rulers and subjects, and institutions that enforce law and order. A student insists the two words mean exactly the same thing. The teacher replies that they do not, and sets the class to sort them out for themselves.

(a) State what the first word stands for, and name the structural units and institutions out of which it is built. (b) Explain what regulates a society, and why this is not the same as the basis of a State. (c) Two large groups can live side by side for generations without ever becoming a State; explain what had to happen in society before such political systems could develop.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) A system of social relationships among individuals sharing a common territory, culture and shared sense of belonging; structural units such as families or households, institutions such as marriage, and customs. (b) Society is primarily regulated by customs and practices rather than formal laws, whereas a State is based on rules and laws. (c) Such political systems developed gradually as societies became larger and more complex.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.topic: Understanding Early Indian State and Society
questions.stem:
An exhibition has been planned on the earliest Indian past, but the curator cannot put a single date on the wall for the oldest hymns. Scholars keep arguing about when they were composed, and the estimates run from the fifth millennium BCE to the second millennium BCE. The museum knows only that these hymns were recited out loud for several centuries before anyone wrote them down. Even more puzzling, the script of the Harappans of the Sindhu–Sarasvatī civilisation has still not been deciphered, so what those people left behind cannot be read. A visitor asks whether the exhibition should be dropped altogether.

(a) State the range of estimates that historians give for the date of composition of the Ṛigveda. (b) Explain why the Vedas are called the earliest known corpus of Indian literature, and state how Vedic literature came to be written down. (c) The curator still wants the exhibition; explain what can be worked out about the Ṛigveda and the Sindhu–Sarasvatī civilisation despite the undeciphered script.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Estimates range from the fifth millennium BCE to the second millennium BCE. (b) The Vedas are the earliest known corpus because the Harappan script is still undeciphered; Vedic literature existed in oral form for several centuries before it was written down. (c) The Ṛigveda was composed in the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent, where the Sindhu–Sarasvatī civilisation flourished, and both were familiar with copper.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.topic: Understanding Early Indian State and Society
questions.stem:
A group of Class 9 students is making a short film on how India was governed in the earliest times, and they keep making the same mistake. One of them says that the earliest groups of people already had a fully formed State with laws and institutions to enforce them. Another says that nobody governed anybody at all. The teacher points out that what the two have to work out is not a single moment but a process: rules and shared norms that maintain order and harmony, and then, much later, organised political systems with rights and duties of rulers and subjects.

(a) State how rules and shared norms come into being, and what they do. (b) List the elements a State includes, and explain the condition in society under which such political systems developed. (c) Only two minutes of film are left; explain why discovering customs and practices alone would not be enough to show that a State existed.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Rules and shared norms evolve over time to maintain order and harmony, binding social groups into a unified whole. (b) A State is an organised political system based on rules and laws, with rights and duties of rulers and subjects and institutions for enforcing law and order. (c) Customs alone prove nothing, since society is primarily regulated by customs and practices rather than formal laws.

evidence: shared norms evolve over time to maintain order and harmony.

a ‘State’ refers to an organised
political system based on rules and laws. It includes well-defined
rights and duties of rulers and subjects, mechanisms of governance,
and institutions for enforcing law and order.

perspective, such political systems developed gradually as societies
became larger and more complex.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
On an outline map of India, locate and label the following:
(a) Kannauj, the main capital of the Gurjara–Pratihāras, in modern-day Uttar Pradesh.
(b) Aihole, a Brahmin settlement to which the Chālukyas gave land grants and which developed into a prominent centre of learning.
(c) Badami, a Brahmin settlement to which the Chālukyas gave land grants and which developed into a prominent centre of learning.
(d) Northern India, the northern part of the large region ruled over by the Gurjara–Pratihāras.
(e) The region of southern India, where the early Cholas formed a powerful kingdom and where King Karikala was found.

markingPoints.description: Kannauj — the main capital of the Gurjara–Pratihāras, in modern-day Uttar Pradesh (1)
Aihole — an agrahāram, a Brahmin settlement to which the Chālukyas gave land grants, which developed into a prominent centre of learning (1)
Badami — an agrahāram, a Brahmin settlement to which the Chālukyas gave land grants, which developed into a prominent centre of learning (1)
Northern India — part of the large parts of Northern and Western India ruled over by the Gurjara–Pratihāras (1)
southern India — the region in which the early Cholas formed a powerful kingdom and King Karikala was found (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
(a) Kannauj — the main capital of the Gurjara–Pratihāras, in modern-day Uttar Pradesh.
(b) Aihole — one of the agrahārams, Brahmin settlements to which the Chālukyas gave land grants, which gradually developed into prominent centres of learning.
(c) Badami — one of the agrahārams, Brahmin settlements to which the Chālukyas gave land grants, which gradually developed into prominent centres of learning.
(d) Northern India — large parts of Northern and Western India were ruled over by the Gurjara–Pratihāras.
(e) southern India — the early Cholas were a powerful kingdom of southern India, and the famous King Karikala belonged to it.
